items.prompt: A runner runs flat out every day and each run was a great run. What does her slower season show?
choices: Some of her runs were too short to really count
The cost of each hard run lands later, outside that run
Running every single day is always harmful to anyone, whatever the effort
items.explanation: The bill arrives in a later period, so no single run shows the damage.

items.prompt: What is long-horizon sustainability?
choices: Working fewer hours than everyone else for as long as possible
Pacing effort over years with planned recovery
Saving all of your effort for one big final push at the end
items.explanation: It means varying intensity on purpose over years, not minimizing effort.

items.prompt: Is a single hard push a mistake?
choices: No, a deliberate push is often the right call
Yes, any push damages the decade
Only if it lasts longer than a week
items.explanation: The mistake is treating every stretch as a push with nothing to repay it.

items.prompt: Which is closer to a marathon pace than a sprint pace?
choices: Maximum effort held at every moment for years on end
Effort that varies on purpose over a long span
A single burst followed by nothing
items.explanation: A marathon runner spreads effort across the whole distance.

items.prompt: What is recovery debt?
choices: Hours of sleep you have saved up to spend later on
Money spent on a vacation after a very hard project
The gap between recovery needed and recovery got
items.explanation: Unpaid recovery compounds and eventually comes due.

items.prompt: In the demo, ten years with zero recovery quarters per push produced how many modeled units?
items.explanation: Skipping recovery gave 18 units, compared with 40 when recovery matched the push.

items.prompt: Why can a quarter look fine while the decade fails?
choices: Quarters are measured much too strictly in most reviews
The cost shows up in a later quarter, not the one that caused it
Decades are always worse than quarters no matter how they are paced
items.explanation: A cost that lands later never appears in the quarter that borrowed it.

items.prompt: Decade-horizon thinking asks which question?
choices: What does this choice do to ten years of output?
Will this impress anyone at review?
Can I survive this quarter?
items.explanation: It evaluates a choice by its long-run effect, not the current cycle.

items.prompt: When is the recovery season supposed to be planned?
choices: Before the push starts
Once the push is already over
Whenever things finally calm down
items.explanation: Planning it in advance is what makes it a commitment.

items.prompt: What does a planned recovery season usually look like?
choices: Lower-stakes work, less on-call, more reflection
Zero work of any kind for months at a time
The same load but with a slightly shorter lunch break
items.explanation: It lowers intensity rather than stopping all output.

items.prompt: A recovery quarter is skipped 'just this once.' What happens to the debt?
choices: It disappears since nothing visibly went wrong
It rolls forward and adds to the next push
It is paid back automatically by the next quarter
items.explanation: Skipped recovery stacks on what the next push borrows.

items.prompt: What does 'sized to the push' mean?
choices: Recovery is always one week
Recovery is as long as possible
Recovery matches what the push borrowed
items.explanation: In the demo, a two-quarter push needs two recovery quarters.

items.prompt: Which plan is a real seasons model?
choices: A promise to rest after the next launch ships
Resting in any quarter where the roadmap happens to look empty
A recovery quarter on the calendar before the push begins
items.explanation: The other two plans depend on nothing else coming up.

items.prompt: In the demo, how many recovery quarters per push gave the highest 10-year output?
items.explanation: Two quarters matched the push and gave 40 units; 0 gave 18 and 4 gave 34.

items.prompt: What happens when something more urgent can always override recovery?
choices: It becomes a permanent push with a hopeful label
It becomes an even stronger seasons model overall
It makes recovery shorter but it stays fully real
items.explanation: Conditional recovery effectively never happens.

items.prompt: In the demo, did taking 4 recovery quarters beat taking 2?
choices: Yes, more rest always gave more output
No, it gave up a little output (34 versus 40)
They gave exactly the same total, 40 each time
items.explanation: More than the push needs adds nothing in the model.

items.prompt: What does spare capacity make possible?
choices: Closing more tickets in a single sprint
Being reachable at every hour of the day and night
Reflecting, teaching and noticing early warnings
items.explanation: Judgment, mentoring and early notice all need slack.

items.prompt: Which is something raw hours mainly buy?

Trust built slowly over several years
Better judgment about which problems to solve
items.explanation: Hours add short-term output but not the compounding parts.

items.prompt: How is trust usually built over years?

By being predictable over years
By taking every request
items.explanation: Predictability, not constant availability, builds lasting trust.

items.prompt: Why does mentoring need slack?

It is mostly a social break from real work, not output
It takes unhurried time a full calendar squeezes out
items.explanation: Mentoring raises others' output but is the first thing a full calendar drops.

items.prompt: A permanently redlined person tends to have what?

More capacity, because they work more hours than others
The same capacity as anyone else on the team

choices: Taking a long weekend off to rest
Naming the pattern as a multi-year one

items.prompt: Priya handed her on-call lead role to someone else. What else did that do?

It gave another engineer a growth opportunity

She ignored the request and never replied to it

items.prompt: What did she put on the calendar as fixed time?

A second project
Mentoring and design review

items.prompt: How late was her promotion compared with the original plan?

Three years
Four months

It would have hurt her standing in the review
items.explanation: The same allocation of work would rebuild the same debt.

items.prompt: What does structural change mean here?
choices: Resting a little harder than before
Looking for a new employer in the same field
Changing how future work is allocated
items.explanation: Rest treats the symptom; allocation treats the pattern.

items.prompt: Did the delayed promotion mean recovery cost her?
choices: Yes, it ended her career
No, it was small next to the alternative trend
It cost her exactly nothing
items.explanation: The promoted version had already shown what recovery made room for.

items.prompt: Two engineers each work ten years. One runs every quarter hot with no planned recovery; the other alternates pushes with recovery matched to each push. Both can point to strong quarters. Which statement about the first engineer's problem is accurate?
choices: Some individual quarters must have been run badly, and a stricter review would have caught that
The damage arrives in the same quarter as each push, so a monthly check would have shown it
The damage depends mainly on total hours, so cutting hours in any one quarter would have fixed it
The damage is a property of the whole sequence, so no single quarter's review would show it
items.explanation: Each quarter looked defensible; the cost lands later, so it is visible only across the sequence. Hours alone are not the issue, and the damage is not in the quarter that caused it.
items.reference:
Same effort, different decade (modeled, 40 quarters)
🔥 0 recovery quarters per push: 18 units
🌤️ 1 recovery quarter per push: 25.5 units
🌱 2 recovery quarters per push: 40 units
Why: the cost of running hot lands in a later quarter, so a decade can fail even when every quarter looked strong.
items.learnMore:
Quarter-optimal is not decade-optimal

Each hot quarter borrows focus, judgment and patience from the next one. Because the bill arrives later, no single quarter shows the damage; only the sequence does.

Common mistake

Checking whether this quarter's push was justified, instead of asking when the recovery that pays it back will happen.
items.reflection: Think of a stretch in school, sport or work where every week felt justified. When did the cost first show up, and in which later week?

A good reason for a push cancels the debt it creates, provided the outcome shipped on time

items.prompt: A team lead says, 'We have a seasons model: we rest whenever there is a gap between projects.' Using this unit's model, what is wrong with that plan?
choices: Recovery depends on nothing else being urgent, so it effectively never happens
Resting between projects is too frequent, so the push seasons never get enough time
Gaps between projects are always the wrong length for a two-quarter push
It confuses rest with output, since gaps between projects already count as work
items.explanation: A real season is planned before the push and protected. A conditional gap disappears whenever something is urgent.
items.reference:
What the seasons model requires
🗓️ Recovery planned before the push starts
📏 Sized to the push (2 quarters for a 2-quarter push in the demo)
🛡️ Protected once it arrives, even when something is urgent
Why: skipped recovery does not cancel; the debt rolls forward and stacks on the next push.
items.learnMore:
Planned, sized, protected

"I will rest when things calm down" is conditional on nothing else being urgent, which for a demanding role is almost never. A season is a commitment made in advance, matched to what the push borrowed.

Common mistake

Assuming more rest is always better; in the demo, taking more than the push needs gives up a little output without gaining any.
items.reflection: Where in your own life is rest currently "when things calm down"? What would it take to put it on the calendar before the next busy stretch?

⏱️ Being always available

The parts of experienced work that compound through other people (choosing the right problem, mentoring, being predictable) are the first things a full calendar squeezes out. Hours measure effort spent, not these.

items.learnMore:
Fixing the pattern, not the week

Naming the problem as three years without recovery, not one bad month, is what makes the next steps possible. A recovery season can also be someone else's growth, and a short delay in advancement is usually small next to the alternative trend.

Common mistake

Taking a long weekend and returning to the same workload.
items.reflection: Imagine a close friend described a similar multi-year pattern. Which one structural change would you suggest first, and what would it cost them?
